title: Housing insecurity is splitting along income, age, race, disability, mobility, and insurance lines
source_unit: Federal Reserve Board, Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025, Housing section
geography: United States; nationally administered household survey with income, age, race/ethnicity, disability, region, renter, and homeowner comparisons

observations.period: 2025; tenure and homeownership by income and demographic group

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Federal Reserve household economic well-being survey

overall_homeownership.unit: percent of adults who owned their home

low_income_homeownership.unit: percent of adults with family income below $50,000 who owned their home

high_income_homeownership.unit: percent of adults with family income of $100,000 or more who owned their home

mechanism.value: Housing tenure is a balance-sheet and place resource that is distributed with income, age, race, disability, and accumulated opportunity

observations.method: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking analysis of housing tenure and demographic characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is cross-sectional and self-reported; tenure differences do not isolate the effects of income, age, inheritance, local prices, credit, or prior mobility.
observations.subgroup: Adults by family income, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, renters, homeowners, and adults living rent-free or with family.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower-income homeownership may rise with age, paid-off homes, family transfers, public programs, or lower-cost geographies; current income alone is not a complete affordability measure.

observations.period: 2025; current housing payments and recent movers

denominator.unit: U.S. homeowners with a mortgage and renters reporting positive monthly payments

median_mortgage.unit: dollars median monthly mortgage payment among homeowners with a mortgage

median_rent.unit: dollars median monthly rent among renters reporting positive rent

recent_mover_mortgage.unit: dollars median monthly mortgage among homeowners who moved in 2024 or 2025

recent_mover_rent.unit: dollars median monthly rent among renters who moved in 2024 or 2025

regional_spread.value: Recent-mover mortgage and rent payments were highest in the West and Northeast and lower in the Midwest and South

mechanism.value: Moving can reset housing costs upward, turning mobility into a financial exposure rather than a route to opportunity

observations.method: Federal Reserve survey estimates of monthly mortgage and rent payments, stratified by recent move and Census region.
observations.uncertainty: Payments are reported medians and do not measure housing quality, income burden, utilities, household sharing, or whether moves were voluntary.
observations.subgroup: Recent movers, renters, mortgaged homeowners, households in the West and Northeast, and people relocating under constrained housing supply.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recent movers may choose higher-cost homes or regions in exchange for better jobs, schools, safety, or amenities; higher payment is not necessarily worse welfare.

denominator.unit: U.S. renters in the Federal Reserve household economic well-being survey

behind_on_rent.unit: percent of renters behind on rent at some point in the prior year

low_income_arrears.unit: percent of renters with family income below $25,000 behind on rent

high_income_arrears.unit: percent of renters with family income of $100,000 or more behind on rent

eviction_or_threat_move.unit: percent of renters who moved in the prior year because of eviction or threat of eviction

mechanism.value: Rent arrears convert income volatility into housing instability, forced mobility, and possible loss of place-based social and work connections

observations.method: Federal Reserve survey questions on rent arrears, income, and reasons for moving.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported arrears and eviction threats are not administrative eviction records; the survey does not establish duration, repayment, displacement distance, or downstream outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Renters, especially those with family income below $25,000, renters facing income shocks, and households relying on local housing and employment networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some renters recover arrears without moving, and some moves following eviction threats may lead to safer or more affordable housing; the measure captures exposure, not total welfare effect.

observations.period: 2025; homeowners insurance, weather exposure, and underinsurance

denominator.unit: U.S. homeowners and adults reporting financial effects from natural disasters or severe weather

uninsured_homeowners.unit: percent of homeowners without homeowners insurance

weather_affected_adults.unit: percent of adults financially affected by a natural disaster or severe weather event in the prior year

low_moderate_neighborhood_uninsured.unit: percent of homeowners in low- or moderate-income neighborhoods without homeowners insurance

cost_reason.unit: percent of uninsured homeowners citing inability to afford insurance as the main reason

underinsurance_preference.unit: percent of insured homeowners preferring more coverage but unable to afford it

mechanism.value: Climate and insurance costs can turn homeownership from a buffer into an uncovered exposure, especially where household assets are concentrated in the home

observations.method: Federal Reserve survey analysis of homeowners insurance status, premium affordability, neighborhood income, and recent weather-related financial effects.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not verify policy terms, replacement values, claims, hazard probabilities, insurer availability, or future losses; weather exposure is self-reported.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income homeowners, homeowners in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, owners with limited assets, and households in severe-weather regions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some uninsured homeowners may face low perceived risk or own homes free and clear; insurance coverage is not the same as full recovery after a disaster.

related_sources.claim: Full Federal Reserve Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025.
Federal Reserve survey description and methodology.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. housing route from tenure and payment burdens through renter arrears, forced mobility, insurance affordability, weather exposure, and household balance-sheet risk. It is a cross-sectional Federal Reserve survey, not an administrative eviction or insurance-claims dataset, a causal housing-market evaluation, or proof of long-term displacement.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Federal Reserve housing page was reviewed for tenure, income, demographic, regional payment, renter-arrears, eviction-mobility, homeowners-insurance, and weather-exposure findings.
